Central Nervous System
Histology
Meninges&Barrier,Neuroglia

This lesson covers the supporting structures of the nervous system: the neuroglial cells of the CNS and PNS, myelination in the CNS and PNS, and the three meninges with the choroid plexus. It ends with the brain barriers (blood-brain, blood-CSF and brain-CSF) that protect neural tissue and stabilise the CSF.

Neuroglia

Neuroglia are cells with metabolic activity that provide mechanical support and protection for neurons. They do not synapse with other cells and do not conduct impulses. They are present in both the CNS and the PNS.

  • CNS: astrocytes, oligodendroglia, microglia, ependymal cells.
  • PNS: Schwann cells, satellite cells.
CellSiteKey featuresFunctions
AstrocytesCNS: protoplasmic in gray matter, fibrous in white matterLargest glial cell; stellate with many processes that envelop blood vessels (perivascular feet) or neurons; cytoplasm rich in intermediate filamentsStructural and metabolic support of neurons; control the ionic and chemical environment; share in forming the blood-brain barrier and in CNS repair
OligodendrogliaCNS: gray and white matterIrregular branched cells with few short processes; small, rounded, condensed nucleus; cytoplasm with ribosomes, microtubules, many mitochondria, extensive RER and a large Golgi complexForm the CNS myelin sheath, which is necessary for survival of the surrounded neurons
MicrogliaCNS: gray and white matterArise in bone marrow from monocytes (mononuclear phagocytic system); small spindle cells with scanty basophilic cytoplasm and dense elongated nuclei; short, branching, spiny processesPhagocytic and antigen-presenting cells
Ependymal cellsLine the central canal of the spinal cord and the brain ventriclesCuboidal; ciliated in certain brain regions (cilia aid CSF movement); continuous with the cuboidal epithelium of the choroid plexusSecretion of CSF; contribute to formation of the choroid plexus
Schwann cellsPNSWrap peripheral axonsForm the PNS myelin sheath; maintain viability and normal function of the axon; regeneration after nerve injury
Satellite cellsGangliaSmall cells forming a thin layer around the nerve cell bodyProtection, insulation and nutrition

Myelination

In the CNS

  • The processes of an oligodendrocyte wrap several nerve fibers in a spiral manner, forming myelin sheaths.
  • Unlike Schwann cells in the PNS, the oligodendrocyte cytoplasm does not form a neurolemmal sheath.

In the PNS

  1. The Schwann cell encircles the axon and rotates several times around it, forming a series of layers, each made of two layers of cell membrane.
  2. The cytoplasm is gradually squeezed out, and the lipid layers of the two membranes fuse to form the lipid component of the myelin sheath.
  3. The membrane layer in contact with the axon is the internal mesaxon; the one in contact with the Schwann cell is the external mesaxon.

Node of Ranvier: the gap between two adjacent Schwann cells. It is not covered by myelin, only by processes of the Schwann cells.

Meninges

The brain and spinal cord are surrounded by three closely associated connective tissue membranes: the dura mater (outermost), the arachnoid (intermediate) and the pia mater (inner).

Dura mater (pachymeninx)

  • Dense connective tissue, loosely attached to the inner surface of the skull except at the sutures and skull base, where it is firmly attached.
  • Outer periosteal layer: osteoprogenitor cells, fibroblasts and bundles of collagen fibers.
  • Inner meningeal layer: fibroblasts and fine collagen fibers. Internal to it lies the border cell layer (fibroblasts and amorphous material).
  • At certain locations the two layers separate to form the venous dural sinuses.
  • Around the spinal cord, the dura is separated from the vertebral periosteum by the epidural space (fat and a venous plexus); the subdural space separates the dura from the arachnoid.

Arachnoid

  • A delicate, nonvascular connective tissue membrane between the dura and the pia.
  • Two components: a flat sheet-like membrane in contact with the dura, and a system of trabeculae (modified fibroblasts, collagen and some elastic fibers) enclosing cavities, the subarachnoid space, which is filled with CSF and communicates with the ventricles of the brain.
  • Arachnoid villi: extensions of the arachnoid through the dura that protrude into the venous sinuses, covered by endothelial cells. They return CSF from the subarachnoid space to the blood of the venous sinuses.

Pia mater

  • A delicate, highly vascular connective tissue layer closely covering the surface of the brain and spinal cord; it follows the convolutions and extends into the depth of the sulci.
  • It conveys small blood vessels into the substance of the CNS.
  • It does not touch neural tissue, because a thin layer of neuroglial processes is always interposed.
  • Composed of flattened modified fibroblasts (resembling arachnoid trabecular cells), macrophages, mast cells, and fine collagenous and elastic fibers.

The arachnoid-pia interface is difficult to distinguish, so the two layers are often called the pia-arachnoid or leptomeninges.

Choroid plexus

  • Folds of pia mater extending into the lateral, 3rd and 4th ventricles.
  • A connective tissue core, highly vascularized with fenestrated capillaries, covered by simple cuboidal or columnar epithelium (ependymal cells) with many microvilli.
  • Produces CSF, which fills the ventricles, the central canal of the spinal cord and the subarachnoid space.

Brain Barriers

These barriers protect the brain tissue and CSF from harmful substances that may enter the bloodstream.

Blood-brain barrier (BBB)

  • Components: continuous (non-fenestrated) capillary endothelium with tight junctions; the basal lamina of the endothelial cells; and astrocyte foot processes that completely envelop the endothelial cells.
  • Functions: separates the blood from the brain tissue and protects it from toxins and other substances that may interfere with normal neuronal function.

Blood-CSF barrier

  • Components: blood capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelial cells; the basal lamina of the endothelial cells; the basal lamina of the ependymal cells; and the ependymal epithelium joined by tight junctions.
  • Functions: separates the blood from the CSF and maintains the chemical stability of the CSF and the difference in composition between CSF and plasma.

Brain-CSF barrier

  • Subarachnoid CSF is separated from brain tissue by the flattened fibroblasts of the pia mater, their elastic and collagenous fibers, and condensed neuroglial cells beneath the pia.
  • Ventricular CSF is separated from brain tissue by ependymal cells connected by tight junctions, their basal lamina, and neuroglial processes.

Key Points / Quick Review

Neuroglia

  • Support and protect neurons; no synapses, no impulse conduction.
  • CNS: astrocytes, oligodendroglia, microglia, ependymal cells. PNS: Schwann and satellite cells.
  • Astrocytes: protoplasmic (gray), fibrous (white); perivascular feet; BBB and repair.
  • Microglia: bone marrow monocyte origin; phagocytic and antigen-presenting.
  • Ependymal cells: line ventricles and central canal; secrete CSF.

Myelination

  • CNS: oligodendrocyte wraps several fibers; no neurolemmal sheath.
  • PNS: Schwann cell rotates around one axon; internal and external mesaxon.
  • Node of Ranvier: gap between adjacent Schwann cells, covered only by their processes.

Meninges

  • Dura (outer): periosteal and meningeal layers, border cell layer; layers split to form venous sinuses.
  • Arachnoid: trabeculae and subarachnoid space (CSF); villi return CSF to venous sinuses.
  • Pia: vascular, follows sulci; neuroglial processes interposed. Pia-arachnoid = leptomeninges.
  • Epidural space: fat and venous plexus; subdural space: between dura and arachnoid.

Choroid plexus and barriers

  • Choroid plexus: pial folds, fenestrated capillaries, cuboidal/columnar epithelium with microvilli; makes CSF.
  • BBB: continuous endothelium with tight junctions, basal lamina, astrocyte feet.
  • Blood-CSF barrier: fenestrated endothelium, two basal laminae, ependymal tight junctions.
  • Brain-CSF barrier: pial fibroblasts and glia (subarachnoid); ependyma and glial processes (ventricles).
